passage: I'm Jomon, and honestly, I didn't see it at first. Rafiq and I have shared a flat since first year. Last spring his school friend Asif went through a terrible breakup, and Rafiq became his everything: calls at two in the morning, skipped classes to sit with him, message after message all day. Then I noticed Rafiq had stopped cooking, stopped playing football, and once fell asleep in the shower. When I asked, he snapped, "If I don't answer and something happens, it's on me." Then he cried, because he also felt guilty for being tired of it. We sat down that night and made a plan. He'd tell Asif, kindly, that he loved him and couldn't be his only person. Asif's brother and the college counsellor would be brought in. Rafiq would keep his phone on silent after midnight unless it was an emergency. It felt harsh to him. It was actually what let him keep helping.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq cry when Jomon asked?
qa.a: He felt guilty for being tired of helping, and afraid that if he didn't answer, anything bad would be his fault.

qa.q: Which part of the plan was hardest for Rafiq, and why was it still a wise choice?
qa.a: Keeping his phone on silent after midnight except in emergencies felt harsh, but it protected his sleep so he could keep helping.

qa.q: What is it like for Rafiq to set these limits?
qa.a: It feels harsh and guilty to him at first, but it gives him rest and shares the load with Asif's brother and the counsellor, so he isn't drained.

grounding: It shows Jomon noticing a young man becoming a friend's only support, drained and guilty, and helping him set kind limits and bring in others.

passage: I'm Omkar. I sit next to Jyoti at the design studio, so I saw most of it, though I can only guess what she felt. From June, she spent every lunch break in the stairwell on the phone, speaking softly: "I know, I know, I'm here." Her friend was going through something bad; that much she told me. By August she was eating biscuits for lunch and her eyes looked puffy most mornings. Once, when her phone buzzed during a client meeting, she went pale and apologised to everyone twice. In September something shifted. I overheard her say, "I care about you, and I can't be the only one. Can I call your mum with you tonight?" After that she took her full lunch break with us. Last Friday she even laughed at the terrible canteen dal. I don't know everything that happened, but she looks like she's breathing again.

qa.q: Where did Jyoti spend every lunch break from June?
qa.a: In the stairwell on the phone.

qa.q: What might Jyoti's pale face during the client meeting suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she may have been anxious that her friend needed her, and embarrassed about the interruption.

qa.q: What choice did Jyoti make in September?
qa.a: She told her friend she cared but couldn't be the only support, and offered to call the friend's mum together.

qa.q: How has the change affected Jyoti, as Omkar sees it?
qa.a: Omkar sees her taking full lunch breaks and laughing again, looking as if she can breathe after months of strain.

grounding: It shows Omkar, who sits beside her at work, watching a young woman drained by being a friend's only support, and seeing her recover once she sets a kind limit and involves others.
